A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same benchmark, renamed from ACVUBench to AVUT. The main text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices A–J in v1 and A–K in v2 support comparison. V2's presentation defects do not prevent matching the underlying content.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations in Tables 3–7, modality ablations, confidence-threshold curves, and annotation analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains original model evaluations and adds a transcription ablation and GPT-4o text-shortcut measurements across benchmarks.

M1.justification: V2 adds an algorithmic filtering stage to benchmark construction: GPT-4o receives each question without video under four cyclic answer permutations, and questions answered correctly in all four are removed. This changes the construction procedure beyond v1's human checks for text-answerable questions; the underlying annotation pipeline remains.

E1.justification: V2 newly evaluates questions from VideoVista, TemporalBench, NExT-QA, MLVU, MotionBench, Video-MME, MVBench, and Perception Test under text-only conditions. It also adds a detailed-transcription input scenario. The original benchmark's eight tasks, 18 domains, and English-video coverage remain; reduced question counts concern E3.

E2.justification: The model comparators in the corresponding MCQ and open-ended experiments remain identical in Tables 3, 4, 6, and 7. The new shortcut study uses the already evaluated GPT-4o; Table 5 adds a modality ablation rather than a new baseline model.

E3.justification: V2 introduces text-only testing, four-permutation cycled accuracy, and a detailed-transcription control, while removing confidence-thresholded accuracy. Reported AV-Human/AV-Gemini question counts change from 2,100/11,674 to 1,734/9,875 following filtering. These are substantial reported protocol changes, although the PDFs do not establish whether retained model scores were recomputed.

E4.justification: V2 adds a cross-benchmark diagnostic of text shortcuts and extends Gemini's modality ablation to test whether detailed transcripts substitute for audio. It removes v1's three-model confidence-threshold sensitivity and calibration analysis. The counting/localization case studies and MCQ-versus-open-ended analysis are retained.

E5.justification: V1's prediction-confidence and calibration reporting through CTA curves and expected calibration error disappears in v2. This concerns predictive confidence rather than uncertainty across experimental repetitions: neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds Table 8's shortcut results, including AVUT's 25.32% text-only and 1.89% cycled accuracy, and Table 5's 69.23% transcription-condition accuracy. V1's CTA findings and ECE range of 0.049–0.122 are removed. All numerical scores in Tables 3, 4, 6, and 7 are unchanged; this does not establish unchanged performance on the newly filtered dataset.

T1.justification: V1's Equations (1)–(3), defining normalized option probabilities, the correct-versus-incorrect probability margin, and CTA, are removed. V2 instead describes cycled accuracy's all-four-correct criterion in prose. This is a localized change to mathematical metric definitions; neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion recast the contribution as an audio-centric benchmark without text shortcuts. V2 newly claims the first systematic investigation of this problem and promotes permutation filtering as a central contribution. V1's confidence-thresholded evaluation claim disappears, while the audio-centric task suite remains central.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of textual cues, memorized associations, and inflated benchmark scores, and interprets the transcription ablation as evidence that audio conveys information beyond transcripts. It removes the explanation linking Qwen2's confidence behavior to its newer backbone and reduced hallucination. The existing limitations concerning older models, short videos, annotator bias, and four-option questions remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix K identifies Gemini 1.5 Pro as the transcription generator and provides an example with timestamps, speaker identities, appearance descriptions, and transcripts. The abstract changes its resource disclosure from demos to demos and data. Existing inference settings, hardware, timing, and prompt templates are retained; online resource availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work against prior benchmarks by emphasizing text shortcuts and claiming the first systematic investigation, rather than primarily emphasizing missing audio-centric annotation. It adds citations for TemporalBench, MotionBench, VideoVista, and MLVU, and removes CrossCheckGPT with the confidence analysis. Most of Section 2's existing survey remains.

P1.justification: V2 renames the benchmark throughout, selectively rewrites the abstract and contribution framing, and condenses annotation-quality prose. It inserts the text-shortcut section and Appendix K while retaining most existing prose and section order. Six experimental table references become unresolved 'Table ??' references.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 8 and a transcription listing, expands Table 5, removes v1's CTA plot, and relocates the domain chart to Appendix A. Result-table captions move below the tables, and Table 2's caption is partially clipped in rendering. The pipeline and case-study illustrations retain their content despite renumbering.

improvement.justification: The shortcut audit, filtering procedure, and transcription ablation add useful checks of benchmark validity. However, v2 reduces the reported dataset from 13,774 to 11,609 questions without clarifying whether unchanged main scores concern the filtered data. Table 8 also reports TemporalBench's cycled accuracy as 73.57%, above its 65.42% text-only accuracy, without explaining the protocol distinction. These unresolved empirical issues, alongside lost confidence analysis and presentation defects, prevent a reliable judgment of net quality improvement.
